In thirty years of practice, I have learned one thing about bad news. Clients forgive the news. What they do not forgive is finding out late. So when a deadline is missed, my first call is to the client, before the internal meeting and before anybody has written a report. I tell them what happened in the first sentence. If we made the mistake, I say so: we should have caught this, and we didn't. What I never do is speculate in front of the client. I do not say the court must have lost the document, or the other side might have changed the date, unless I know it is true. Guessing sounds like an excuse. Then, and only then, I give them the plan: what we are doing today, what it will cost, and who is paying for it. Most of the time, the client stays. The ones who leave are the ones who heard it from somebody else.

The worst conversation of my career happened about ten years ago. We had lost an appeal for a client, a family business, and I had to tell the owner. I was so worried about her reaction that I tried to soften the blow. I talked for ten minutes about the judge, the timing, the arguments that almost worked. She listened very patiently, and then she said: you should have told me in the first minute. I could have started thinking about the next step ten minutes ago. She was right. She must have known from my face as soon as I walked in. Now, when I have bad news, I say it first, in one sentence, and then I stop talking. The silence is uncomfortable, but it belongs to the client, not to me.

First, Pedro finds out that the termination notice was never sent. Then he checks every inbox to be sure before he says anything. Next, he calls Nora and breaks the news in the first sentence. After that, Nora asks him to say the notice was sent in March, and he refuses. Finally, he proposes a plan to renegotiate the price with the distributor.
